NEW DELHI: With CJP-led protests over NEET-UG 2026 examination irregularities showing no signs of easing, Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Thursday said the government would take stricter action against paper leaks."Friends, I know that paper leaks are not an ordinary matter. For lakhs of students and their parents, it is extremely painful," PM Modi said in a self-recorded video posted on X.PM Modi said the Union Cabinet would consider a draft Bill proposing Fast-Track Courts and stringent punishment for offenders."In the last two and a half months since the paper leak incidents, several major steps have been taken. The culprits have been caught; they are currently in jail," he added.PM Modi highlighted that the government made every effort to ensure that the students did not lose an academic year."Our most important responsibility was to ensure that a whole year for the students is not wasted. It was very important to conduct the exams immediately. The government used its full strength to arrange exams for nearly 22 lakh students in the shortest possible time. And just five or six days ago, on the 19th, the results were also announced.News of the happiness of successful students is coming from all over the country. "PM Modi said that the government has decided to take stronger measures to tackle paper leaks."However, we are not among those who are satisfied with just that. And therefore, today I have issued directions to the departments to set up Fast-Track Courts. The departments worked tirelessly and, late last night, provided me with a draft. This draft, which includes provisions for Fast-Track Courts and stringent punishments, will be discussed in the Cabinet tomorrow," he added."After incorporating suggestions from Cabinet colleagues, it will be given a final shape. Efforts will be made to get this Bill passed in the House as soon as possible, as the second week of the Parliament session begins on Monday," he said.The PM also urged activist Sonam Wangchuk to follow doctors' advice, recover well and gain weight as soon as possible."I urge Sonam ji to follow his routine as per the doctors' advice and regain his old weight as soon as possible. I pray to the Lord that Sonam ji remains healthy," he said in a post on X.Activist Sonam Wangchuk ended his 26-day hunger strike on Friday at Medanta Hospital in the presence of Union ministers J P Nadda and Jitendra Singh, along with senior leaders of the Apex Body of Leh Ladakh.In a post on X, Wangchuk said he decided to call off the fast after prolonged negotiations on various conditions and in view of the possibility of violence in the country.The Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), which has been spearheading the protest at Jantar Mantar, welcomed Wangchuk's decision but said its agitation would continue until Union Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan resigns.
Article Summary: PM Modi said the Union Cabinet would consider a draft Bill proposing Fast-Track Courts and stringent punishment for offenders. Activist Sonam Wangchuk ended his 26-day hunger strike on Friday. The Cockroach Janta Party welcomed Wangchuk's decision but said its agitation would continue until Union Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan resigns.

Article Title: IndiGo opposes more say for airport operators in airlines
Article Text:
Rahul Bhatia, promoter and MD of India’s largest carrier IndiGo

NEW DELHI: Rahul Bhatia, promoter and MD of India's largest carrier IndiGo , has opposed the proposed move to allow airport operators in India to own and run airlines too. "There is no global precedent for this. It raises massive conflict-of-interest concerns, and it is unclear how such a move would serve consumers' interests," he said at a post earnings call.Bhatia's Thursday comments come as govt is considering to dilute provisions that disallow operators of Delhi and Mumbai airports to own more than 10% stake in a scheduled airline. While the Adani Group, which runs Mumbai airport, is likely to make the first move by picking up stake in an existing airline or investing in a startup, the GMR Group, which operates Delhi's IGIA, could do so at a subsequent stage.The news has resulted in Interglobe Aviation's shares falling for two consecutive days as investors perceive the airline, which controls two-thirds of the domestic aviation market, to be a loser in case the move goes through.Senior aviation ministry officials said a country with the economic potential of India should have multiple airlines and not just a duopoly with IndiGo and Tata's Air India group.Meanwhile, the Competition Commission of India (CCI) Thursday invited public comments on a commitment proposal by IndiGo in a probe following its last Dec schedule collapse.The airline has proposed temporarily releasing domestic slots at airports. "Post such handover, the airport operator/authority may determine re-allocation of such slots/dates for routes, as deemed fit," the CCI notice says.
Article Summary: Rahul Bhatia, promoter and MD of India's largest carrier IndiGo, has opposed the proposed move to allow airport operators in India to own and run airlines too. "There is no global precedent for this. It raises massive conflict-of-interest concerns, and it is unclear how such a move would serve consumers' interests," he said.

Article Title: CJP, Centre set for 12:30 pm talks at Constitution Club; Pradhan's resignation among key demand
Article Text:
CJP-Centre meeting to be held today (ANI)

'Peaceful protest will continue'

NEW DELHI: The Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) delegation will meet Union ministers at the Constitution Club of India at 12.30 pm on Friday, after the Centre agreed to hold talks at a neutral venue—a key demand raised by the outfit during its ongoing agitation over the NEET row.The meeting comes a day after activist Sonam Wangchuk ended his 26-day hunger strike at Medanta Hospital in the presence of Union ministers JP Nadda and Jitendra Singh, paving the way for formal discussions between the government and the protesters.Confirming the development, CJP chief spokesperson Saurav Das said the organisation welcomed the government's decision to shift the talks to a neutral venue."Our protest will continue; Constitution Club of India chosen as venue for meeting with government ministers, hoping for an open-minded dialogue," Das told reporters on Thursday.CJP spokesperson Vaishnavi Gaur said the delegation would place the same demands it has been raising since the protests began."We will be putting forward our demands, which we have been consistent with from the first day," she said.According to Gaur, the key demands include the resignation of Union education minister Dharmendra Pradhan, compensation for the families affected by the NEET controversy, and withdrawal of all FIRs registered against what she described as "innocent protesters."Following Wangchuk's decision to end his fast, CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke thanked him for what he called an extraordinary act of courage."We are relieved and grateful that Sonam sir has ended his hunger strike after 26 days. Thank you for your extraordinary courage and sacrifice. By putting your own life on the line, you awakened the conscience of an entire nation. Your life is far too precious to this country," Dipke wrote in a post on X.Despite Wangchuk ending his fast, the CJP has maintained that its peaceful protest at Delhi's Jantar Mantar will continue until its demands, including Pradhan's resignation, are addressed.
Article Summary: Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) delegation will meet Union ministers at the Constitution Club of India at 12.30 pm on Friday. Meeting comes a day after activist Sonam Wangchuk ended his 26-day hunger strike at Medanta Hospital.

Article Title: 20-year-old US student, army officer's son, dies as car plunges into open drain in south Delhi
Article Text:
The circumstances that led to the crash are being probed, say police





NEW DELHI: A 20-year-old student home from US was killed when the car he was driving overturned and plunged into an open drain in south Delhi's Vasant Kunj early Friday.A young woman travelling with him escaped from the vehicle and survived.The victim was identified as Yashvendra, who recently returned to India and was staying with a friend in Delhi Cantonment area. His father is an Army officer posted in Kolkata.The accident took place around 6am near the Nangal Dewat drain. Police teams pulled the vehicle out of the drain and dragged out Yashvendra. He was taken to a hospital, where doctors declared him brought dead.Police said because of rain the road where the car crashed was slushy. It might have caused the car to skid, hit a tree, overturn and fall into the drain, they said.The girl, in a statement to police, too, blamed the slippery road for the accident.The drain had no cover or retaining wall to prevent vehicles or pedestrians from falling into it.“Yashvendra was accompanied by his friend, a woman, who is also studying in the same business school as him in the US. They were coming towards Mahipalpur from a friend’s house in Vasant Kunj Enclave.It is suspected that he lost control of the vehicle when he took a sharp turn,” a senior police officer said.The vehicle belongs to the woman, but Yashvendra was driving. The woman was able to get out of the car as she was able to open the door on her side after the car fell in the drain. The officer said the man, however, was stuck inside and the roof of the vehicle also completely collapsed. The woman suffered minor injuries.A case has not been registered yet, police said.The circumstances that led to the crash, including the speed of the vehicle and whether any other factor contributed to the accident, are being probed. CCTV footage from the area is also being examined.
Article Summary: A 20-year-old student home from US was killed when the car he was driving overturned and plunged into an open drain in south Delhi's Vasant Kunj early Friday. A young woman travelling with him escaped from the vehicle and survived. The circumstances that led to the crash are being probed, say police.

Article Title: Florida scientists used female Burmese pythons as live lures to find invasive males in the Everglades, but 3 million camera-trap photos produced only four python detections
Article Text:
Conservancy biologists with a 16ft, 135lb female Burmese python found while radio-tracking a male scout snake in southwest Florida in February 2025.

Southeastern Naturalist

Captivity stress and chemical signals

The ongoing battle in the Everglades

Removal programs and public support

Florida scientists used female Burmese pythons as live lures to find invasive males in the Everglades, but 3 million camera-trap photos produced only four python detections.A study published in the journalshows that placing wild-caught female Burmese pythons (Python bivittatus) in cages across the Greater Everglades Ecosystem failed to draw in wild males.Over a 90-day field test at 12 locations, researchers filtered more than three million camera-trap photos using artificial intelligence software. They recorded just three python visits at the cages holding female lures and one visit at empty control cages.The study, titled "Not so fatal attraction: Captive female Burmese Python lures do not improve wild python detection," was written by Alex D. Potash, Maggie Jones, Michael Kirkland, Jenna Cole, Kristen Hart, and Robert A. McCleery. The research record was published by the USGS Publications Warehouse and carried out through the USGS Wetland and Aquatic Research Center.In controlled laboratory settings, male pythons show a strong interest in the scents given off by breeding females. However, the scientists suggest that the stress of living in cages may have stopped the captive females from releasing pheromones, removing the chemical scent needed to attract wild males.Understanding how pythons communicate is still limited. The authors note that finding better care methods to reduce stress in captured females could improve future tests, while further work on python chemistry might help create fake scents to track the invasive snakes.The failed female lure test follows another setback with scent tracking. In an August 2025 study published in Management of Biological Invasions, titled "Mammalian scent lures fail to increase detections of invasive Burmese pythons (Python bivittatus)," researchers tested whether rabbit scent could replace live prey.Written by Storm Miller, Michael Kirkland, Kristen Hart, and Robert A. McCleery of the USGS Wetland and Aquatic Research Center, the 84-day experiment across 21 sites brought only 11 python sightings. Four pythons were seen near rabbit scent lures (poop, urine, and hair) and seven near plain soil. While the rabbit scent attracted more native snakes by drawing in live mice and rats, it did not draw in pythons.These scent experiments show how hard it is to find a top predator that has wiped out native mammals like marsh rabbits, foxes, raccoons, and deer.Pythons spread through South Florida in the 1990s when escaped or released pets entered the wild. Today, tens of thousands live in the wetlands. Females can lay up to 100 eggs a year, making control efforts urgent.Despite scent lure challenges, state teams and conservation groups report steady progress through hunting and radio tracking.The Conservancy of Southwest Florida recently announced it has removed 20 tons of pythons from the wild over a decade, setting a single-season record by taking 6,300 pounds of snakes out of a 200-square-mile area since November.The conservancy's main strategy relies on fitting wild male "scout" snakes with radio trackers during the November-to-April breeding season. The tagged males lead biologists straight to breeding groups, allowing teams to catch large females before they lay eggs.“There’s very good evidence that the scout snake program is our most effective and least biased method. It doesn’t just limit us to targeting human accessible areas and it’s super targeted toward those reproductive females,” said Andrew Durso, a herpetologist at Florida Gulf Coast University. “But it’s expensive to radio-track these males into remote parts of the Everglades where you can’t go very easily. You need air support from a helicopter, which ups the price per python removed. It’s all a balance sheet of how do we want to spend money?”Ian Bartoszek, science project manager and chief wildlife scientist at the Conservancy of Southwest Florida, noted that his team's work has stopped roughly 20,000 eggs from hatching since 2013.“Through years of research we’ve developed science-based methods to track this apex predator more effectively and mitigate its damage to our native wildlife population,” said Bartoszek. “Burmese pythons are impressive creatures that are here from no fault of their own. As wildlife biologists, we have tremendous respect for all snake species. However, we understand the impact invasive pythons are having on the biodiversity in our area and we humanely remove them from the ecosystem. ”The South Florida Water Management District has separately tracked and removed over 15,650 pythons through its Python Elimination Program, which hires paid snake hunters. Public support stays high, aided by annual events like the Florida Python Challenge, which drew 895 hunters who caught 195 pythons in 2024.Mike Kirkland, python program manager at the district, sees signs that removal work is helping key areas.“Every single python that’s removed is positive for the environment,” said Kirkland. “We’re getting better and better at removing this invasive species. We’re learning more about their behavior and life history, and their non-native range here in south Florida, which is leading to more removals and hopefully innovation and novel strategies going forward.”Kirkland added that removing every single python across the wetlands may not be possible, but local populations are changing.“Progress is being made. Anecdotally we’re seeing some demographic shifts, and regionally, we’re seeing less larger size-class pythons in certain areas. That’s a direct result of our management efforts, and our partners’ management efforts,” Kirkland said.“As with most environmental issues, a multi-pronged strategy of different efforts working in concert with one another is really the best path forward,” Kirkland added. “In the future I see the python population being greatly reduced, and to a point where we can begin to see a robust return of our native animal populations, which is why we’re doing all this to begin with. I’m confident we’re going to be able to manage this species to the point where we’re seeing our deer populations, our foxes, our possums, our raccoons and so on, restored to the Everglades. ”Burmese pythons (Python bivittatus) are among the world's largest snakes, commonly growing 10–16 feet (3–5 metres) long, with some exceeding 18 feet (5.5 metres). Native to Southeast Asia, they are non-venomous constrictors that kill prey by cutting off blood flow before swallowing it whole using flexible jaws. They can eat animals as large as deer and alligators, then survive for weeks or even months without another meal. Females may lay more than 100 eggs in one clutch and protect them until they hatch. In Florida's Everglades, where they are invasive, Burmese pythons have caused major declines in several native mammal populations.
Article Summary: Florida scientists used female Burmese pythons as live lures to find invasive males in the Everglades, but 3 million camera-trap photos produced only four python detections. The stress of living in cages may have stopped the captive females from releasing pheromones, removing the chemical scent needed to attract wild males.

Article Title: In the 1980s, Scotland planted commercial trees across parts of a 9,000-year-old peatland; decades later, conservationists are removing them to protect wildlife and keep its stored carbon in the groun
Article Text:
A Common Greenshank stood on the edge of a pool of water.

Destruction of a wild habitat

A Common Greenshank stood on the edge of a pool of water.

Reversing the damage at Forsinard Flows

Government backing and broader targets

Bringing communities into the bog

In the 1980s, Scotland planted commercial trees across parts of a 9,000-year-old peatland; decades later, conservationists are removing them to protect wildlife and keep its stored carbon in the ground.The massive project centers on the Flow Country, a vast area of wet bog covering over 400,000 hectares across Caithness and Sutherland in northern Scotland. In July 2024, UNESCO named the area a World Heritage Site, placing it alongside natural treasures like the Great Barrier Reef and the Grand Canyon. It became the world's first peatland to get this special status. King Charles III marked the event by visiting the Royal Society for the Protection of Birds (RSPB) Forsinard Flows reserve to reveal a special plaque.Despite its global fame today, large parts of this ancient landscape were nearly ruined forty years ago. During the 1980s, tax rules and government grants encouraged forestry companies to drain the wet ground, build deer fences, put in roads, and plant long rows of commercial trees.The quick growth of these tree farms hurt the delicate bog. The trees pulled water out of the muddy ground, causing the deep peat soil to dry out and break down.This loss of open land threatened local birds that need wide, treeless spaces to build their nests. Before government action stopped the planting, the region lost about 900 pairs of Golden Plovers, nearly 800 pairs of Dunlins, and 130 pairs of Greenshanks. The area is also a vital home for Hen Harriers, insect-eating sundew plants, Common Scoters, and Red-throated Divers, which lay eggs near small bog pools.Pressure from the Nature Conservancy Council, the RSPB, and other green groups eventually forced the government to change its plans. In January 1988, Malcolm Rifkind, who was then Secretary of State for Scotland, announced that the government would protect over 140,000 hectares of peatland as Sites of Special Scientific Interest. Later that year, Nigel Lawson, then Chancellor, ended the tax breaks and grants that made tree planting on peat profitable.Real cleanup work started in 1994 when the RSPB bought the Forsinard Estate in the middle of the Flow Country, paid for by donations from its members. Today, RSPB Forsinard Flows is the largest nature reserve managed by the charity in the UK.Using money from two big European Union LIFE Nature grants, conservation teams tested ways to cut down the commercial trees, block drainage ditches, and soak the ground again. The main goal is to turn thousands of cleared hectares back into healthy, working bogs.The choice to cut down trees goes beyond helping wildlife. Peatlands are often called the lungs of the Earth because they absorb and trap carbon. The Flow Country alone holds roughly 400 million tonnes of carbon in its soil, which is more carbon than all of the UK’s forests and woods combined. When peat dries out, that trapped carbon leaks back into the air as heat-trapping gas.Peatlands cover over two million hectares across Scotland, making up 25 per cent of the country's land area and more than 60 per cent of all UK peatlands.To help fix this land, the Scottish Government promised £250 million over ten years to restore 250,000 hectares of damaged peatlands by 2030 through its Peatland ACTION Programme. Official records show that over 75,000 hectares have been fixed so far, including a record 10,360 hectares completed during the 2023-24 financial year.Scotland's peatland policy focuses on three main steps: protecting healthy sites, taking care of working land, and fixing damaged areas. New science shows that other practical steps, like keeping farm animals and deer from overgrazing, re-wetting farm soil, and changing how grassy peatlands are used, can cut gas emissions even further.Fixing remote peatlands means working in tough conditions, where cold weather and wet mud make field tasks hard. To gain public and political support, conservation groups built better visitor spots at Forsinard Flows.The reserve now features a Lookout Tower that gives visitors a wide view of the open landscape. New investments have added modern research rooms and housing on site, letting scientists, researchers, and volunteers live at the reserve while studying how healthy bogs trap carbon and bring back rare birds.Beside storing carbon and creating homes for wildlife, the Scottish Government sees peatland repair as a way to create green jobs. The long cleanup effort is bringing countryside work to northern Scotland, helping local hotels and cafes, and building up green tourism.
Article Summary: Peatlands cover over two million hectares across Scotland, making up 25 per cent of the country's land area. The Flow Country alone holds roughly 400 million tonnes of carbon in its soil, which is more carbon than all of the UK’s forests and woods combined. When peat dries out, that trapped carbon leaks back into the air as heat-trapping gas.

Article Title: Vietnam moves to bar under-16s from posting, commenting on social media
Article Text:
Poll Vote & Share your view Do you support the idea of requiring social media accounts for children under 16 to be registered through a parent or guardian? Yes, it enhances safety No, it restricts freedom 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Vietnam is planning to require social media platforms to stop users under the age of 16 from posting content, commenting or reacting to posts, under a draft decree aimed at strengthening online protections for children, according to a document reviewed by Reuters.The proposed rules would require social media accounts belonging to children under 16 to be registered using the information of a parent or legal guardian, who would be responsible for supervising the content viewed by children and the amount of time they spend on the platforms.The draft decree also requires social media companies to use technical measures to identify child users and ensure that they receive age-appropriate content. Platforms would have to provide the highest level of privacy protection for child accounts and proactively detect, warn and block access to content related to violence, pornography, gambling, drugs, suicide and other harmful material."The primary objective is not to ban or excessively restrict children's access to social media, but rather to ensure that when children use social media services, they are placed in an age-appropriate environment and protected from inappropriate risks," deputy culture minister Phan Tam said on Thursday during a meeting to discuss the proposed rules.The proposal comes as governments across the world tighten regulations on children's use of social media amid growing concerns over online safety and the impact of harmful content on young users' mental health.Earlier this week, French lawmakers approved a ban on social media access for children under 15. Australia became the first country to impose such a ban, while several other countries are considering similar measures.The draft decree also proposes new restrictions on online gaming by minors. Game operators would be required to verify users' ages, register accounts of children under 16 through a parent or legal guardian, and limit users under 16 to a maximum of 60 minutes of gameplay per day across games offered by the same company.The draft decree has not yet been finalised and may be revised before it is formally adopted.
Article Summary: Vietnam is planning to require social media platforms to stop users under the age of 16 from posting content, commenting or reacting to posts. The draft decree is aimed at strengthening online protections for children. The proposal comes as governments across the world tighten regulations on children's use of social media.

Article Title: Inside Tuvalu: This tiny island nation has just one airline, almost no tourists, and a future threatened by rising seas
Article Text:
Why Tuvalu is considered one of the most vulnerable nations on earth

What NASA's analysis actually found

A rising tide already visible on the ground

Daily life on a shrinking runway between the ocean

A cash economy that only recently modernised

Why a nation this small carries such outsized stakes

Tuvalu is one of the least visited countries on earth. A single airline, Fiji Airways, operates the only scheduled flights in and out, connecting the capital atoll of Funafuti to Fiji a few times a week, and there is no other way to reach the country by air. The entire nation is made up of nine coral atolls covering roughly 26 square kilometres, smaller than many major airports, and is home to just under 11,000 people. Life here has always moved differently from most of the world, shaped by close communal ties and a cash-based economy that only recently saw its first ATMs installed. But scientists now warn Tuvalu faces a far bigger question than isolation: whether the country will remain habitable at all as sea levels continue to rise.Tuvalu's islands sit at an average elevation of only about two metres above sea level, among the lowest of any country on the planet. According to a technical report titled Assessment of Sea Level Rise and Associated Impacts for Tuvalu , produced by NASA 's Sea Level Change Team in support of the United Nations-backed Rising Nations Initiative, Tuvalu has already begun experiencing measurable impacts from the combined effects of rising oceans, storms and natural ocean variability, effects the report expects to worsen in the years ahead.According to NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory , Pacific island nations including Tuvalu, Kiribati and Fiji will experience at least 15 centimetres of sea level rise over the next 30 years, a figure the agency describes as effectively locked in regardless of whether global greenhouse gas emissions change going forward. The analysis was carried out by researchers at the University of Hawaii, working alongside scientists from the University of Colorado and Virginia Tech, at the request of Pacific island governments themselves, and in coordination with the United States Department of State. Nadya Vinogradova Shiffer, who directs ocean physics programs within NASA's Earth Science Division, noted that sea levels will continue rising for centuries, bringing more frequent flooding to coastal communities across the region regardless of near-term emissions decisions.Grace Malie, a youth leader from Tuvalu involved with the Rising Nations Initiative, told NASA that accurate science and data can help her community understand exactly what these sea level projections mean in practice, adding that this information also supports early warning systems the country is actively developing. Malie described the stakes bluntly, saying the future of Tuvalu's young people is already at stake, and that climate change represents a matter of justice and survival rather than simply an environmental concern. NASA researchers noted a genuine shortage of on-the-ground measurement data in Pacific nations like Tuvalu, which is part of why the agency has begun combining satellite-based sea level data with ground station measurements and more detailed land elevation mapping specifically for these vulnerable coastlines.Despite the scale of the threat it faces, Tuvalu remains almost entirely disconnected from global tourism. Fiji Airways is the sole carrier serving the country, and flights operate only a few times each week between Funafuti and Fiji, making Tuvalu one of the hardest countries in the world to simply visit. Funafuti International Airport itself is modest by international standards, a single terminal building sitting so close to the surrounding village that locals can walk directly onto the runway whenever no flight is scheduled.Until quite recently, every transaction in Tuvalu, by locals and visitors alike, had to be conducted entirely in cash, since the country had no ATMs anywhere on its islands. That changed in April 2025, when the National Bank of Tuvalu, the country's only bank, installed the nation's first five ATMs on Funafuti, including machines at Vaiaku village and the airport itself. Prime Minister Feleti Teo described the moment as a significant milestone for the country, while the bank's general manager, Siose Teo, called it a transformative switch that would open doors to broader economic participation for Tuvaluans. Even with this change, banking infrastructure across the country remains extremely limited compared to almost anywhere else in the world.Whatever infrastructure changes come next, the core threat facing Tuvalu remains the same one NASA's sea level science team has been documenting for years: a slow, largely irreversible rise in sea level that threatens not just periodic flooding but the long-term habitability of the country itself. With no natural elevation to retreat to and limited land available for adaptation, Tuvalu has become one of the clearest real-world test cases for what rising seas mean for entire nations, not just coastlines, making its quiet, rarely visited atolls a subject of growing scientific and diplomatic attention far beyond their tiny population and remote location in the middle of the Pacific.
Article Summary: Tuvalu's islands sit at an average elevation of only about two metres above sea level, among the lowest of any country on the planet. Pacific island nations including Tuvalu, Kiribati and Fiji will experience at least 15 centimetres of sea level rise over the next 30 years.

Article Title: Iran war risk: JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon warns of oil shocks, sticky inflation and higher interest rates
Article Text: JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon has warned that the ongoing war in Iran could trigger oil and commodity price shocks, keeping inflation elevated and pushing interest rates higher than current market expectations, Reuters reported.The warning came in his annual letter to shareholders, a day after US President Donald Trump escalated pressure on Iran by threatening to target key infrastructure if the Strait of Hormuz is not reopened."Now, because of the war in Iran, we additionally face the potential for significant ongoing oil and commodity price shocks, along with the reshaping of global supply chains, which may lead to stickier inflation and ultimately higher interest rates than markets currently expect," Dimon said, news agency Reuters quoted as saying.Dimon, who has led JPMorgan for two decades, also highlighted broader geopolitical risks, including the war in Ukraine, tensions in the Middle East and friction with China."The challenges we all face are significant," he added.He said it remains uncertain whether the Iran war will achieve US objectives, while warning that nuclear proliferation remains the biggest risk linked to Iran.Markets have already begun pricing in these risks, with expectations of interest rate cuts this year largely fading amid rising inflation concerns triggered by the conflict.Last week, the benchmark S&P 500 index recorded its worst quarterly performance since 2022, weighed down by rising energy prices and geopolitical uncertainty since late February.Dimon noted that the US economy remains resilient, with consumers continuing to earn and spend, and businesses staying broadly healthy, though signs of weakening have emerged.He cautioned that economic strength has been supported by significant government deficit spending and past stimulus, while infrastructure investment needs continue to grow.At the same time, he pointed to positives such as fiscal stimulus under President Trump's "Big, Beautiful Bill", deregulation policies and rising capital expenditure driven by artificial intelligence.On financial stability, Dimon said the $1.8-trillion private credit market "probably" does not pose a systemic risk, despite investor concerns and recent withdrawals from such funds.However, he warned that in a downturn, losses across leveraged lending could exceed expectations as credit standards have weakened.Private credit markets also lack transparency and rigorous valuation benchmarks, increasing the risk of investor exits if conditions worsen, he said.Separately, Dimon criticised revised US capital rules, including Basel III and GSIB surcharge norms, calling aspects of the proposals "nonsensical" and "very flawed".He said JPMorgan’s GSIB surcharge would fall only to 5.0%, a level he described as “absurd” and “un-American”, arguing it penalises the bank’s scale and performance.
Article Summary: JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon warns Iran war could trigger oil and commodity price shocks. He also highlighted broader geopolitical risks, including the war in Ukraine, tensions in the Middle East and friction with China. Dimon criticised revised US capital rules, including Basel III and GSIB surcharge norms, calling aspects of the proposals "nonsensical"

Article Title: How selling Alaska in 1867 was a costly mistake for Russia
Article Text:
Image: Wikipedia

Why Russia agreed to the Alaska purchase

The hidden wealth Russia gave away

Strategic and geopolitical consequences







In 1867, Russia’s decision to sell Alaska to America turned out to be a historic mistake that was to go unnoticed for years to come. The sum paid by the US was only $7,200,000. Although, in the light of the circumstances at the time, it appeared logical, retrospectively, the act looks extremely shortsighted. Russia found itself economically constrained, geographically far away from the region and fearful of its falling into the hands of the British without any compensation. In reality, however, the region had proved immensely valuable both strategically and naturally. Its vast reserves of oil, gold, and natural resources would later transform it into one of the most economically significant territories in the United States.The choice of selling Alaska was based on economic and political reasons. By the middle of the 19th century, the Russian Empire experienced financial difficulties as a result of the expensive Crimean War. It had become increasingly hard for the country to manage such remote and thinly populated areas as Alaska.According to EBSCO , “the Russian-American Company was in decline, and the colony failed to yield any profit”.In addition to this, the lucrative fur trade had declined, making the territory much less economically valuable for the empire.At the same time, Russia was afraid that Britain might capture Alaska in case another war broke out between the two countries. Selling the colony to the friendly United States appeared as a logical step. As the Office of the Historian states, William H. Seward, U.S. Secretary of State, “it was a chance to expand its influence in North America and hinder further growth of Britain”.For Russia, the transaction was a chance to minimise the losses. However, it greatly undervalued the potential of Alaska.Another thing that Russia did not expect was the amount of riches that Alaska possessed. Within several decades after the acquisition, the state saw discoveries of enormous deposits of gold, oil, and other minerals.“Alaska has produced more than 40 million ounces of gold,” according to the US Geological Survey. Furthermore, Alaska is home to some of the world's most significant undeveloped mineral deposits, according to the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) . But even more importantly, the state's oil deposits turned out to be extremely valuable. The Prudhoe Bay oil field was discovered in 1968 and became one of North America's biggest.In retrospect, the amount paid by the Americans, $7.2 million, or two cents per acre, was rather laughable. According to Howard I. Kushner , the deal “robbed Russia of an enormously rich territory, the true value of which would only be recognised in the twentieth century.”In addition to resources, there is the question of strategy and how important Alaska is to the United States from a strategic standpoint. This is a very good place when it comes to defence strategy. It borders on the Arctic Ocean and also happens to be close to Russia.During the period of the Cold War, the Alaskan region became a frontier area for the United States, becoming home to military facilities and warning systems.According to Col. Michael J. Forsyth, U.S. Army, the closeness of Russia and Alaska, only about ninety kilometres apart across the Bering Strait, meant that this region became highly significant to the United States' defence plans.From today's point of view, the strategic location of Alaska makes the state very important to the policies of the U.S. related to the Arctic, energy security, and even environmental policies.Thinking back, what seems clear to us now is that the Russians sold Alaska due to immediate needs rather than future considerations. In order to solve the problem, they lost a valuable resource for Russia.Conclusively, the Alaska Purchase should not have been done as it has had a significant impact that will remain throughout history.
Article Summary: Russia sold Alaska to the U.S. in 1867 for only $7,200,000. The sale was based on economic and political reasons. However, the region proved immensely valuable both strategically and naturally. Alaska is home to some of the world's most significant undeveloped mineral deposits. The Prudhoe Bay oil field was discovered in 1968.

Article Title: AI data centers are causing 'stress' not just to tech companies, but also private insurers
Article Text:
Massive investments, growing risks



Unique challenges for data centre insurance companies





AI data centers are reportedly putting new pressure on the insurance industry. According to a CNBC report, experts warn that the rapid growth of these projects is becoming a “stress test” not just for tech companies, but also for private insurers and lenders. Consulting firm McKinsey estimates that global spending on data centers could reach $7 trillion by 2030. As costs rise, tech giants are increasingly relying on private equity, private credit and debt to fund these projects. The scale of investments is creating challenges for insurers.“When you put $10 to $20 billion plus in a single location, it creates capacity issues in the marketplace,” said Tom Harper, data center leader at insurance broker Gallagher as quoted in the CNBC report.He added that the sector has been a “real stress test” over the last few years, as insurers struggle to provide coverage for such large and complex projects. While these facilities are seen as high-quality assets, Harper said insuring them has become difficult due to their size and risk concentration.Private data center deals have crossed $10 billion regularly, with some reaching as high as $40 billion. Companies including Nvidia, Microsoft and BlackRock have already taken part in large investment deals.Rajat Rana, partner at Quinn Emanuel Urquhart & Sullivan, described the scale as unprecedented. “We’re talking about trillions of dollars, and almost going back to the same cycle where there’s almost no transparency about the financing structures — the scale is astronomical,” he said. He added that the boom in AI data centers could be “the largest peacetime investment project in human history.”Experts say the way these projects are financed is adding another layer of risk. Much of the funding is happening through complex and less transparent debt structures. Rana warned that this trend feels like “deja vu,” referring to past financial cycles. He said the lack of transparency could create risks for investors, insurers and pension funds.As stated in the CNBC report, data centers offer unique challenges due to their mix of real estate and advanced technology. Insurers are now designing custom policies to manage these risks. However, challenges remain. Large facilities are often located in areas prone to extreme weather, and they store expensive equipment, sometimes even before installation.Another key concern is the mismatch between the lifespan of data centers and the hardware they use. While data centers can last decades, GPUs — the chips powering AI — typically last around seven years. Rana described this as a “GPU debt treadmill,” saying, “This is almost like a treadmill that these AI data centers are running on.”He explained that companies may need to keep raising debt to upgrade infrastructure as technology evolves.
Article Summary: Private data center deals have crossed $10 billion regularly, with some reaching as high as $40 billion. McKinsey estimates that global spending on data centers could reach $7 trillion by 2030. Tech giants are increasingly relying on private equity, private credit and debt to fund these projects.

Article Title: 2 hours, 3 demands, 5 reform suggestions: Govt seeks time for call on Dharmendra Pradhan exit demand
Article Text:
Centre agreed to no action on protesters: CJP after talks





Sugandha.Jha1New Delhi: Representatives of Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) held a second round of talks with the Centre Friday, following which the govt sought time till Saturday afternoon to respond to their demand for Union education minister Dharmendra Pradhan 's resignation. CJP reasserted its agitation would continue till the demand was met.The meeting, held at Constitution Club, was attended by Union ministers J P Nadda and Jitendra Singh . The CJP delegation comprised spokespersons Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka."We hope the govt will remove him (Pradhan) soon," Ranka said after the meeting.At Jantar Mantar, CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke said Pradhan's exit would be in the govt's best interest. Given the anger among protesters, he said, if Pradhan doesn't resign, demands could begin for the resignation of the PM instead, and CJP would launch an agitation bigger than the July 20 march.Das, meanwhile, said the govt was positive on two other demands. "The govt expressed in-principle approval on the two demands for Rs 1 crore compensation to each of the families of NEET aspirants who died by suicide, and withdrawal of FIRs and legal cases against students," he said. The delegation had been invited for another round of discussions Saturday afternoon, Das added.CJP said it had submitted a memorandum to the Centre reiterating three principal demands: Pradhan's resignation, Rs 1 crore compensation for NEET suicide victims' families, and no action against protesters who participated in the July 20 march.Sources said 47 personnel have been terminated, not merely transferred or marked for removal. Their names, ranks and alleged ro-les were not disclosed. Cases indicating criminal wrongdoing will be referred to appropriate agencies, while departmental and legal proceedings will follow separately.The assessment and psychometrics vertical head will oversee question banks, normalisation, equating and calibration, and computer-adaptive testing and AI-assisted assessment. The test-centre operations head will supervise NTA 's network across more than 500 cities and select overseas centres, including empanelment, capacity, accessibility, amenities, exam day operations and coordination with administrations.The information security head will serve as chief information security officer, responsible for systems, networks, applications, candidate data, a round-the-clock security operations centre and compliance with data protection, information technology and CERT-In requirements. The vigilance, investigation and forensics head will lead malpractice inquiries, build in-house digital forensics capability and coordinate with CBI, Intelligence Bureau, ED, state police forces and cybercrime units under Public Examinations (Prevention of Unfair Means) Act, 2024.The Pratibha Setu - Professional Resource and Talent Integration Bridge for Hiring Aspirants - platform gives verified employers access to willing candidates who cleared stages of UPSC exams but were not recommended in the final merit list.Twelve positions will be in academic research, two in legal research and two in finance and accounts. The appointments will be for 24 mo-nths, and extendable to 36 mo-nths based on performance.The changes seek to reduce NTA's dependence on temporary manpower. It has 39 sanctioned permanent posts, all on deputation, but only 24 are filled, against 73 contractual personnel and 124 outsourced workers.Further hiring will follow across 10 functional verticals recommended by the Radhakrishnan committee. NTA has also initiated fresh empanelment of subject experts and translators.The overhaul will accompany changes to exam delivery. NEET-UG will shift from OMR-based testing to computer-based testing from 2027, bringing it closer to JEE Main and CUET. The move should reduce physical movement of papers, enable multiple question sets and create a digital trail, but will require secure centres, stronger cybersecurity and safeguards against technical failures.Govt is also reviewing outsourcing in registration, centre management, technology services and handling of confidential material. The new model will define responsibility, strengthen audits and background checks, reduce agencies handling sensitive information, and impose tougher penalties for security failures.
Article Summary: Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) held a second round of talks with the Centre Friday. The govt sought time till Saturday afternoon to respond to their demand for Union education minister Dharmendra Pradhan's resignation. CJP reasserted its agitation would continue till the demand was met.

Article Title: 63 lakh city voters mapped under SIR
Article Text: NEW DELHI: Nearly 63 lakh enumeration forms have been filled, returned and verified under Special Intensive Revision (SIR) 2026 of the electoral rolls in the city. According to the SIR report dated July 24, the digitisation of the returned forms has crossed the 40% mark.The report showed that enumeration forms were distributed to 1,44,87,155 of Delhi’s 1,45,10,298 electors, taking the distribution rate to 99.8%. Of them, 62,95,790 forms have been digitised, accounting for 43.4% of the electorate.Among the districts, Outer North has recorded the highest digitisation rate at 55.6%, followed by South West (51.5%), West (47.8%), North West (47.1%) and Central North (46.6%). South East reported the lowest digitisation rate at 27.6%, while East stood at 33.3% and South at 34.2%.“The digitisation of enumeration forms is picking up pace. We are expecting that the number will increase significantly during the weekend,” said an official.The enumeration phase began on June 30 and will continue till Aug 8. During this period, booth level officers (BLOs) are distributing pre-printed enumeration forms carrying voters’ details, which electors must verify, update if required, sign and return.After verifying the information, BLOs map the voters and the forms are digitised. Voters successfully verified during the exercise will be included in the draft and final electoral rolls without having to submit additional documents. The draft roll will be published on Aug 17 and the final roll on Oct 19. Election Commission of India has appointed four senior IAS officers of Delhi govt as electoral roll observers to supervise the revision process, review field-level progress, address procedural issues and ensure that the exercise is carried out uniformly, transparently and in accordance with the poll panel’s guidelines for the preparation of accurate electoral rolls. Each officer has been assigned specific districts and scheduled to conduct three rounds of visits during the revision process.The observers are K Mahesh, secretary (art, culture and language); Pandurang K Pole, secretary-cum-commissioner (labour); Rashmi Singh , secretary (women and child development); and Yashpal Garg, secretary (planning).An official said the observers would make their first visit between Aug 17 and Sept 16, during the period of receiving claims and objections. The second visit will take place between Sept 17 and Oct 15 to oversee the disposal of claims and objections by electoral registration officers. Their final visit is scheduled on Oct 19, when they will supervise verification of the working copy by BLOs, printing of supplements and publication of the final electoral roll.
Article Summary: The digitisation of the returned forms has crossed the 40% mark. Outer North has recorded the highest digitisation rate at 55.6%. The draft roll will be published on Aug 17 and the final roll on Oct 19. Election Commission of India has appointed four senior IAS officers of Delhi govt as electoral roll observers to supervise the revision process.

Article Title: One small step for Hyderabad, one giant leap for Vikram-1
Article Text:
India's first private orbital rocket, Vikram-1, blasts off from Sriharikota carrying four satellite payloads

More than a launch, a signal

Why Hyderabad?





Hyderabad's space ecosystem

Skyroot's rise mirrors Hyderabad's ambitions



Dhruva Space gives the ecosystem another pillar



Policy, capital and research converge



Building beyond rockets



Reforms that changed the landscape



From reforms to orbit





Can Hyderabad overtake Bengaluru?



Race for India's space capital

The challenges ahead



Strengths and challenges





A launch that changed the conversation







HYDERABAD: Skyroot's landmark launch has given India's private space ambitions their biggest boost yet. But can one successful mission transform Hyderabad into the country's spacetech capital, or is the harder journey only just beginning?When Skyroot Aerospace's Vikram-1 pierced the skies above Sriharikota on July 18, it did far more than place four satellite payloads into a 450-km low-Earth orbit.For the first time, a privately developed Indian orbital rocket successfully reached orbit, placing India among a small group of countries, including the United States and China, where private companies have independently designed, built and launched orbital rockets.For Hyderabad, however, the significance stretched well beyond a historic countdown.The city's largest spacetech startup had delivered India's most consequential private space milestone, prompting a larger question: is Vikram-1 merely a breakthrough for one company, or has it accelerated Hyderabad's emergence as the country's private space capital?The answer lies not just in a rocket that flew successfully, but in the ecosystem that made it possible.The symbolism surrounding Mission Aagaman was impossible to miss. Vikram-1 lifted off exactly 46 years after ISRO's SLV-3 placed the Rohini satellite into orbit, marking India's arrival as a spacefaring nation in 1980. This time, history repeated itself under very different circumstances.Instead of a government laboratory, the mission was led by a startup founded only eight years ago by former ISRO scientists Pawan Kumar Chandana and Naga Bharath Daka.Built around an all-carbon composite airframe, equipped with in-house propulsion systems and 3D-printed engines, Vikram-1 demonstrated that Indian private industry had matured from building components to developing complete launch vehicles.Its success also reflected the changing structure of India's space programme. Until a few years ago, orbital launches remained the exclusive domain of ISRO. Today, private companies are beginning to share that responsibility, targeting the rapidly expanding market for small satellite launches.As Skyroot CEO Chandana put it after the mission, the launch proved that India possesses "the talent, the technology and the industrial strength to build launch vehicles that meet the world's standards and serve the world from here."The achievement was not merely technical. It validated years of policy reforms aimed at opening India's space sector to private participation, while giving investors, customers and policymakers confidence that Indian startups can compete in one of the world's most technologically demanding industries.It is tempting to view Skyroot's success as the achievement of one ambitious startup. But Vikram-1 is also a story about geography.Unlike India's traditional space establishment, centred largely around Bengaluru and ISRO's network of research centres, much of the country's emerging private launch ecosystem has taken shape in Hyderabad.The city's credentials extend well beyond one company. It hosts Skyroot Aerospace, satellite manufacturer Dhruva Space, Pixxel's growing presence, specialised component manufacturers, defence and aerospace suppliers, research institutions and one of India's most active startup ecosystems.According to the IIIT Hyderabad Centre for Innovation and Entrepreneurship's SpaceTech Ecosystem Report, Hyderabad has steadily evolved into one of India's leading spacetech clusters, driven by a combination of research institutions, manufacturing capability, venture capital, startup incubation and government support.Rather than relying on a single anchor institution, the city has developed an interconnected network linking startups, academia, investors and industry.The report identifies Hyderabad as one of the country's fastest-growing hubs for downstream and upstream space technologies, with strengths ranging from launch vehicles and satellites to propulsion systems, electronics, data analytics and earth observation applications.This ecosystem is significantly different from the government-driven model that defined India's space sector for decades.Founded in 2018, Skyroot Aerospace emerged at a time when India's private space ecosystem was still finding its footing.Its founders had spent years at ISRO before deciding that India's future space ambitions required private launch capability alongside government missions.Their first milestone came in 2022 with Vikram-S, India's first privately built sub-orbital rocket. Vikram-1 represents a far bigger leap: from reaching space briefly to successfully entering orbit.That journey has been accompanied by rapid institutional growth. The company has attracted more than $160 million in funding from investors including GIC, Temasek, BlackRock and Sherpalo Ventures, while becoming India's first spacetech unicorn.Its newly established Infinity manufacturing facility near Hyderabad airport is expected to eventually support a production cadence of one rocket every month.According to Skyroot Aerospace, the company is also developing the heavier-lift Vikram-II launch vehicle, capable of carrying up to 900 kg to low-Earth orbit (600 kg to Sun-Synchronous Orbit), alongside reusable launch technologies designed to reduce launch costs while scaling manufacturing at its Infinity campus.Together, these reflect its ambition to move from demonstration missions to regular commercial launches.Equally important is what Skyroot has created beyond its own factory floor. The company's maiden orbital mission involved more than 1,000 employees and nearly 400 suppliers across India, illustrating how private launch vehicles require extensive domestic supply chains spanning precision manufacturing, electronics, materials, software and testing.For Hyderabad, that supplier network could prove as important as the rocket itself.If Skyroot represents Hyderabad's launch ambitions, Dhruva Space reflects the city's growing strength in satellite manufacturing.According to Dhruva Space, the Hyderabad-headquartered company has evolved into an end-to-end space engineering firm, offering satellite platforms, payload integration, launch support, mission operations and ground-station infrastructure, illustrating how the city's spacetech ecosystem now extends well beyond launch vehicles.Unlike launch companies that operate mission by mission, satellite manufacturers participate across the broader lifecycle of space programmes, from design and integration to operations.Dhruva's growing manufacturing capabilities, multiple customer missions and continued expansion suggest Hyderabad's spacetech ambitions are not dependent on a single success story.That distinction matters. Globally successful space clusters rarely emerge around one flagship company alone. Silicon Valley is not defined only by Apple, nor Seattle only by Boeing.Sustainable ecosystems are built when specialised companies operate across complementary segments of the value chain. Hyderabad increasingly appears to be moving in that direction.Industry observers often argue that successful innovation clusters require three ingredients: talent, capital and policy support. Hyderabad appears to be assembling all three.The Telangana government's SpaceTech Framework positions the sector as a strategic growth area, focusing on infrastructure creation, startup support, industry partnerships, research collaboration and skill development.The framework aims to build an ecosystem capable of supporting companies across manufacturing, launch services, satellite technologies and downstream applications.Chief Minister A Revanth Reddy has repeatedly described aerospace as one of Telangana's priority sectors, arguing that companies like Skyroot demonstrate the state's growing capabilities in advanced manufacturing and deep technology.The government has also linked aerospace expansion with broader ambitions of positioning Telangana as a global innovation hub by 2047.Research institutions are playing an equally significant role.The IIIT Hyderabad report notes that universities and research centres have become increasingly important in nurturing spacetech entrepreneurship by producing skilled engineers, supporting applied research and connecting startups with investors and industry partners.Instead of operating in isolation, startups benefit from access to a wider innovation ecosystem that encourages experimentation and commercialisation.That ecosystem is further strengthened by Hyderabad's existing strengths in information technology, defence manufacturing, electronics and precision engineering, industries that naturally complement spacetech development.If Skyroot has become the face of Hyderabad's spacetech ambitions, the city is equally betting on the ecosystem that nurtures companies long before they reach the launch pad.Among the most prominent enablers is T-Hub, which has increasingly focused on deep-tech ventures, including spacetech.Through its Orbit SpaceTech programme, launched in collaboration with industry and ecosystem partners, T-Hub aims to help startups working across satellite technologies, downstream applications, manufacturing and space-enabled services move from prototype to commercialisation.While only a handful of startups may eventually build launch vehicles, the broader value chain, from components and electronics to software, analytics and earth observation, offers far greater opportunities for new companies.That approach aligns with Hyderabad's larger strategy of creating an integrated ecosystem rather than relying solely on a few flagship startups.Even the strongest startup ecosystem would have struggled without a policy shift at the national level.The opening of India's space sector in 2020 fundamentally altered the industry's trajectory.The creation of the Indian National Space Promotion and Authorisation Centre (IN-SPACe) provided private companies with a regulatory framework to access ISRO facilities, seek launch authorisations and participate in activities that were previously reserved almost entirely for the national space agency.Skyroot's own founders have acknowledged that ISRO and IN-SPACe played an important role in supporting Mission Aagaman through technical guidance and timely clearances.Following Vikram-1's successful mission, ISRO Chairman V Narayanan described the launch as "the outcome of years of innovation, perseverance and engineering excellence" and said it reflected "the growing maturity of India's private space sector."He added that ISRO and IN-SPACe remained committed to building a globally competitive ecosystem alongside private industry.IN-SPACe Chairman Pawan Goenka echoed that sentiment, calling the launch "an India moment" and noting that more than 1,000 people and nearly 400 suppliers contributed to the mission.The achievement, he said, demonstrated the industrial capability India had developed over the past few years.The pace of growth has been remarkable. According to government data cited by PIB and IN-SPACe, India has gone from having just one recognised space startup at the beginning of the reforms to more than 400 today.While these companies are spread across the country, Hyderabad has emerged as one of the largest beneficiaries of the liberalised policy environment.Yet calling Hyderabad India's space capital today would be premature.Bengaluru remains the country's undisputed institutional centre for space activity.It houses ISRO headquarters, several major ISRO centres, the headquarters of NewSpace India Limited (NSIL), numerous defence laboratories, public-sector aerospace companies and decades of accumulated engineering expertise.Much of India's satellite development, mission planning and advanced research continues to be anchored there.Karnataka's draft Space Policy also seeks to strengthen Bengaluru's long-standing aerospace ecosystem by encouraging commercial manufacturing, private launch capability and downstream space services, underscoring the growing competition among states to attract spacetech investments.The city also benefits from an established aerospace manufacturing base, a mature venture capital ecosystem and one of the country's deepest pools of engineering talent.Chennai, meanwhile, has begun carving out its own niche through companies such as Agnikul Cosmos, which successfully tested its semi-cryogenic Agnibaan launch vehicle.Tamil Nadu's draft Space Policy further signals the state's intention to attract manufacturing, launch support services and private investment.Against these competitors, Hyderabad's strengths are different. Rather than inheriting a legacy government ecosystem, the city has built momentum around private enterprise.Skyroot, Dhruva Space and several emerging startups represent a younger ecosystem that is being shaped alongside policy reforms rather than decades before them.The IIIT Hyderabad report notes that this concentration of startups, investors, incubators and academic institutions gives the city a distinct advantage in commercial innovation.At the same time, it cautions that sustaining growth will depend on strengthening manufacturing capacity, talent pipelines, financing and collaboration across institutions.For all the optimism generated by Vikram-1, Hyderabad's ambitions still face significant hurdles.The first is scale, a single successful launch, however historic, does not establish a commercially proven launch provider.As Skyroot itself has acknowledged, Vikram-1 remains a technology validation mission.Commercial confidence will depend on repeated successful launches over the coming years.Manufacturing presents another challenge.While Hyderabad has developed strengths in aerospace, defence and electronics, building a globally competitive launch ecosystem requires specialised suppliers capable of producing propulsion systems, avionics, composite materials and precision components at scale.Expanding that industrial base will take sustained investment beyond a few high-profile startups.Funding is another critical factor. Space technology remains among the most capital-intensive industries in the world.Developing rockets, satellites and associated infrastructure demands long investment cycles with uncertain returns.Although Skyroot has attracted significant global funding and achieved unicorn status, maintaining investor confidence across the wider ecosystem will depend on commercial success rather than technological milestones alone.Talent, too, will become increasingly important.As more companies enter the sector, competition for experienced aerospace engineers, propulsion specialists, software developers and systems engineers is likely to intensify.Hyderabad's universities and research institutions will have to expand their role in producing specialised talent if the ecosystem is to sustain long-term growth.Infrastructure will also determine whether momentum translates into leadership.Testing facilities, manufacturing clusters, supply-chain resilience, regulatory support and stronger industry-academia partnerships will all be necessary if Hyderabad hopes to compete with established global space clusters.Perhaps Vikram-1's greatest contribution lies not in the payloads it carried into orbit but in the questions it has forced the industry to ask.Until recently, India's private space story centred largely on aspirations.Companies spoke about building rockets, attracting investment and competing globally. Vikram-1 transformed those ambitions into demonstrated capability.For Hyderabad, that distinction matters.The city is no longer simply home to promising spacetech startups; it is home to India's first private company to place an orbital rocket into space, a growing satellite manufacturer in Dhruva Space, a supportive policy framework, active startup incubators, globally recognised research institutions and an increasingly sophisticated network of suppliers and investors.Whether that combination ultimately earns Hyderabad the title of India's space capital remains uncertain.Bengaluru still possesses unmatched institutional depth, while Chennai is steadily strengthening its own launch ecosystem.Leadership in the space economy will not be determined by a single mission or a single company, but by the ability to continuously innovate, manufacture, attract talent and serve a rapidly expanding global market.Vikram-1 has undoubtedly given Hyderabad unprecedented momentum.But the city's claim to becoming India's space capital will ultimately rest not on one historic launch, but on whether it can build an enduring ecosystem where many more such missions become routine rather than remarkable.
Article Summary: India's first private orbital rocket, Vikram-1, blasted off from Sriharikota on July 18. Skyroot Aerospace's landmark launch has given India's private space ambitions their biggest boost yet. Can one successful mission transform Hyderabad into the country's spacetech capital, or is the harder journey only just beginning?

Article Title: Parks plentiful on paper, scarce on ground: Report shows how green are wards in reality
Article Text:
Mumbai's public open space access shows sharp disparities across its administrative wards.

Why your ward determines access to open space.





While satellite images paint Mumbai as a green city, the reality on the ground is stark: public open space ranges from 9.4 sq m per resident in A Ward to just 0.5 sq m in B Ward, exposing sharp disparities in access to parks across the city’s 24 administrative wards.To put this in perspective, residents of A Ward have nearly a parking space’s worth of public open space each, while those in B Ward have barely enough room to stand.The finding is in the report Public Open Space Mapping and Management Strategy for Mumbai by the Urban Design Research Institute (UDRI) and NAGAR (NGO Alliance for Governance and Renewal).Per capita public open space was calculated using the combined area of Existing Open Spaces (EOS) and Reserved Open Spaces (ROS) in DP 2034 against each ward’s 2011 Census population. The report found Mumbai currently has just 1.28 sq m of existing open space per person, far below the DP 2034 target of 4 sq m.The report distinguishes between EOS and ROS earmarked under the Development Plan, noting that even EOS figures do not necessarily reflect actual public access.The study found several existing open spaces remain partly or wholly inaccessible due to encroachments, restrictions, private ownership or limited public access, meaning usable recreational space may be lower than official figures suggest.For instance, a private club in Andheri is marked as a public recreational space despite restricted access, while a school playground in Malad is shown as a public playground even though the public cannot use it.Anuradha Parmar, executive director, UDRI, says, “While acquiring new reserved open spaces remains a challenge, there is no justification for leaving existing ones unusable.The fastest way to increase the city’s usable open space is to urgently channel BMC funds, much of which go unspent each year, towards developing already acquired but neglected open spaces. Equally important is ensuring that every Existing Open Space (EOS) has access through a road formally demarcated in the DP, protecting these spaces from private encroachment.”The report says the island city averages 2.94 sq m of public open space per person, though disparities remain. In the suburbs, the average drops to 1.05 sq m. M East (Govandi), L (Kurla) and H East (Kalina) wards have the poorest access, with 0.6 sq m, 0.6 sq m and 0.7 sq m per capita, respectively. According to the report, these wards face multiple constraints, including high slum density.Nayana Kathpalia, trustee, UDRI and NAGAR, said while every ward has its own challenges and historical legacy, redevelopment in some of Mumbai’s densest neighbourhoods offers a rare opportunity to rethink public spaces and shared amenities. “We need to stop viewing redevelopment as merely a real estate exercise and start treating it as a once-in-a-generation chance to create more open spaces,” she said.Parul Kumtha, also a trustee fromNAGAR, said Mumbai has another major opportunity with the creation of large new public open spaces. “Connecting underserved neighbourhoods to large city-wide assets like the Coastal Road gardens and Mahalaxmi Racecourse is key to expanding equitable access to green spaces.”Reacting to the report, Sunil Rathod, chief engineer of the DP department, said the 4 sq m per capitatarget will be achieved gradually as reserved open spaces are acquired and developed. “Since outright land purchase is not financially feasible, the BMC relies on planning tools under the DCPR, including TDR and redevelopment, while acquiring land where there is a clear public need.”
Article Summary: Public open space in Mumbai ranges from 9.4 sq m per resident in A Ward to just 0.5 sq m in B Ward. Residents of A Ward have nearly a parking space’s worth of public open space each, while those in B ward have barely enough room to stand.

Article Title: Three foreign nationals held with Rs 18 crore smuggled gold hidden inside aircraft panels
Article Text:
The officials said they had intelligence that some passengers would either carry gold on their person or conceal it inside the aircraft





Mumbai: The Directorate of Revenue Intelligence (DRI) has arrested three foreign nationals for allegedly attempting to smuggle over 12 kg of gold worth ₹18 crore by concealing it inside the washroom panels of an international flight arriving from Ethiopia.The three arrested have been identified as Ahmed Abdurahman, 24, Mohammed Abdurahman, 20, and Jemil Nuri Mohammed, 29, who are nationals of Ethiopia. The trio arrived in India from Addis Ababa on Thursday evening.The officials had intelligence that some passengers would either carry gold on their person or conceal it inside the aircraft with the assistance of cleaning staffers at the airport for its subsequent retrieval and illegal clearance.The officials intercepted the trio at the aerobridge shortly after the flight landed. While the accused denied carrying any gold or contraband, personal searches yielded nothing incriminating.However, searches of their cabin baggage led to the recovery of Allen keys from each of the three passengers. During sustained questioning, the accused allegedly admitted that the tools were meant to open aircraft panels and conceal the smuggled gold inside the rear washrooms of the aircraft for later retrieval by cleaning staff.Accused Jemil Nuri disclosed he received six gold bars in Addis Ababa and, after boarding the flight, handed three bars each to the other two accused with instructions to hide them in separate washrooms using the Allen keys. Ahmed Abdurahman and Abdulselam Abdurahman allegedly corroborated the statement and admitted concealing the gold in the left and right rear washrooms of the aircraft.Based on the disclosures, DRI officers escorted the accused back to the aircraft and recovered six yellow metal bars wrapped in brown adhesive tape from the two rear washrooms. A govt-approved valuer certified that the recovered bars were 24-carat gold weighing 12,004 grammes with a total market value of ₹18 crore. If the consignment was imported legally through the baggage route, customs duty of approximately ₹7.92 crore would have been payable, resulting in an alleged duty evasion of about ₹7.92 crore. Their advocate Ravi Hirani, defending them, told the customs court that his clients were unaware of the Indian laws. The court remanded them to judicial custody.
Article Summary: The officials intercepted the trio at the aerobridge shortly after the flight landed. While the accused denied carrying any gold or contraband, personal searches yielded nothing incriminating. However, searches of their cabin baggage led to the recovery of Allen keys from each of the three passengers. The court remanded them to judicial custody.

Article Title: ‘Seven in 10 oral cancer patients reach hospitals too late’
Article Text: Mumbai: As seven out of 10 patients with head-and-neck cancers in India reach hospitals only after the disease has severely advanced, doctors -- ahead of World Head and Neck Cancer Day on July 27 -- underlined the importance of routine screening for oral cancer.The Mazgaon-based Head and Neck Cancer Institute of India (HNCII), along with NGOs Cancer Patients Aid Association, Indian Cancer Society and dentists, on Friday launched an awareness and screening campaign titled ‘In Cancer, Delay Is the Real Killer’.“The idea is to urge people to seek medical attention at the first sign of symptoms rather than postponing diagnosis or treatment,” HNCII founder Dr Sultan A Pradhan said. Head and neck cancers account for nearly 30% of all cancers in India, with tobacco use responsible for the majority of cases.The BMC also last year started screening for oral, cervical and breast cancer, but experts feel wider awareness is needed. In 2025, the BMC screened close to 3 lakh people for oral cancer, identifying 3,000 as suspected cases; 650 biopsies were conducted that further led to 24 patients getting diagnosed with oral cancer.On Friday, Dr Pradhan said, “We have made significant advances in the treatment of cancer, but these advances can only help if patients reach us in time.” Too often, people ignore a symptom, wait for it to disappear, postpone a consultation or delay treatment after diagnosis. “Our message is simple: if something is not right, get it checked. In cancer, delay is the real killer,” he added.People should not ignore persistent mouth ulcers, painless lumps in the neck, difficulty in swallowing or unexplained changes in voice, as these could be early warning signs of oral or head and neck cancers.
